caption:
The FAA is expanding SMART, its AI air traffic planning tool, to all 22 US air route traffic control centers.
In tests around Washington it rerouted about 180 flights, saving about 10 minutes and 80 gallons of fuel each on average.
Controllers still make the final call, but their union says it was not involved in building it.

Would you feel safer or more nervous knowing AI helps plan your flight path?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

Source: Gizmodo · Photo: Kevin Carter / Getty Images
threads_text: The FAA's AI tool that suggests new flight routes is now running in all 22 US air traffic control centers. Early results: about 10 minutes saved per rerouted flight, and controllers can still say no. Would you trust AI to help plan your next flight?

paragraphs.text: The Federal Aviation Administration said on November 10, 2026, that it is now using SMART, an AI assisted air traffic planning tool, in all 22 US air route traffic control centers, according to Gizmodo and Deep Arrival. Gizmodo, citing Ars Technica, said the tool will now assist in managing air traffic across the entire national airspace system.

Gizmodo described SMART as an $875 million system. The FAA first used it for the airspace around Washington, D.C., in September 2026. Deep Arrival reported that the expansion moved from Washington to the Jacksonville, Miami and Atlanta centers before reaching all 22, and that Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has set spring 2027 as the target for full, phased deployment.

According to FAA fact sheets cited by Gizmodo, SMART combines weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow and controller staffing data to predict delays and propose better routes. Deep Arrival described it as a cloud based platform that draws on about 200 data streams. A team of experts in Washington validates the findings before they reach air traffic control, and controllers decide whether to accept or decline each suggestion.

Gizmodo reported that Duffy, citing Politico, has said a human will always manage American airspace. Airlines had worried in September about an abrupt rollout and about the system overcorrecting for predicted delays, but they were relieved that SMART only generates alternative routes that pass through existing FAA systems.

The FAA says SMART has helped reroute about 180 flights, saving an average of about 10 minutes and 80 gallons of fuel per flight. Deep Arrival cited two examples: a flight into Fort Lauderdale with 119 passengers that avoided a 33 minute delay after specialists built a shorter route around forecast storms, and a cargo flight from Tampa that landed at Dallas Fort Worth 12 minutes early after controllers accepted a shorter southern route.

American Airlines chief executive Robert Isom has praised the tool, according to Gizmodo, and The Dallas Morning News reported that he sees it making better use of airspace during weather events, as summarized by Deep Arrival.

The National Air Traffic Controllers Association, which represents more than 15,000 members, said it was not involved in the design, testing or implementation of SMART and cannot speak to its effect on the controller workforce. House Democrats asked the Government Accountability Office to review the tool's rollout, performance metrics and safety risk management, saying frontline staff had little input and limited training and warning that AI could hallucinate safety critical information.
Gizmodo noted that FAA officials had told airlines the full rollout would follow a 90 day test period, and that it is unclear why the agency is moving faster than that timeline.

For NeuraFeed, SMART is one of the clearest cases of AI moving into safety critical government work in the United States. The reported savings are modest compared with the tens of thousands of flights the country handles each day, so the larger test will be whether it reduces weather delays and ground stops without adding risk or workload for controllers.
Watch for the GAO review requested by House Democrats and for FAA data on delays and ground stops as SMART runs through the winter storm season.
